Table of Contents


Toggle


Year-end payroll preparation in Nigeria carries extra weight this December. 2026 was the first full year under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, so the figures you close with cover a year in which the PAYE rules changed while payroll was running: the Consolidated Relief Allowance gave way to a ₦800,000 zero-rate band and rent relief. Your system has probably run consistently all year. The review tells you whether it ran correctly.


This guide follows the 9 checks that bring payroll, bank and accounting records into agreement before the employer annual return falls due on 31 January, and points to where errors tend to sit: the transition months, undocumented reliefs, pension credits that never reached a Retirement Savings Account, and headcount that differs between HR and payroll.


##


**What Is Year-End Payroll Preparation?**


Year-end payroll preparation is the work of reconciling a full year of payroll against bank and accounting records, confirming that statutory contributions were handled correctly, and closing the year with figures you can support, before the employer’s annual return is filed.


Three terms get used interchangeably, and each catches a different kind of error.


##


**Payroll Reconciliation**


Matching payroll reports to bank payments and ledger entries. Our guide to[payroll reconciliation in Nigeria](https://blog.myeazipay.com/2026/08/26/payroll-reconciliation-nigeria/) explains this further.


##


**Payroll Audit**


Reviewing the process behind the numbers: who can change a salary, who approves a run, and which controls exist. See our guide to[payroll audit in Nigeria](https://blog.myeazipay.com/2026/08/31/payroll-audit-nigeria/) .


##


**Payroll Year-End Closing**


Locking the records and producing the figures for the employer annual return and for the first payroll of January.


##


**Why Nigerian Businesses Should Complete a Year-End Payroll Review**


The[Nigeria Tax Act 2025](https://tat.gov.ng/Nigeria-Tax-Act-2025.pdf) took effect on 1 January 2026, so the review should also cover how the new rules were applied month by month, including any weeks when payroll settings were still being updated. Finding those cases now lets you correct them in the December run, ahead of the 31 January return.


Done properly, the review also confirms that salary calculations are right, employee payment records are complete, deductions and remittances agree, and outstanding liabilities and bonuses are documented. That is what your annual return and your year-end accounts rest on.


# **Year-End Payroll Preparation Checklist for Nigerian Businesses**


##


**1. Review Employee Information and Payroll Records**


Start with a headcount: opening headcount plus hires minus exits should equal closing headcount in HR records, in payroll and on the pension schedule.


Then check each file for tax ID, start and exit dates, department, salary structure, bank details and allowances, and match every salary change to a signed approval. Records work is dull, but it is where the rest of the review starts.


##


**2. Reconcile Monthly Salary Payments**


Lay your 12 payroll reports beside the bank statements. Net salary on the report should equal what left the account, and gross pay, overtime, arrears and corrected entries should each trace to a record. A gap of ₦40,000 can be a reversed payment, a duplicate, or a manual transfer that never reached the payroll system.


Set a variance rule while you are at it. Pick a percentage, for example 5%, and investigate any employee whose net pay moved by more than that between months without an approved change.


##


**3. Review PAYE Tax Calculations and Remittances**


PAYE has the most moving parts this year, here are 4 checks:


**Transition months.** Find the first payroll cycle in which your system applied the new rules. If the old relief logic stayed live for even one run, or relief inputs were loaded late, those employees were taxed differently from everyone else. Recompute each employee’s full-year PAYE under the new rules, compare it with PAYE deducted from January to November plus the projected December amount, and sort the differences by size. A few large ones usually share a single cause. Agree the correction method with your tax adviser and the relevant state revenue service before touching payslips.


**December bonuses.** Rebuild the December PAYE for three bonus recipients, once cumulatively for the year to date and once for December alone. If your system’s figure matches neither, the configuration needs fixing. If it matches December alone, expect sharp drops in net pay and queries in January.


**Rent relief coverage.** Rent relief is 20% of annual rent paid, capped at ₦500,000, and the Joint Revenue Board’s 2026 guidelines expect the tenant’s name, rent paid and period covered, the property address, and the landlord’s details. Track one ratio: employees with documents on file divided by employees with relief applied. Where it falls below 100%, apply each person’s marginal rate to the undocumented relief to see the tax at stake, then either collect the paperwork or withdraw the relief in the December run.


**Deducted versus remitted.** Monthly PAYE goes to the State Internal Revenue Service, and states generally work to the 10th of the following month. List each employee’s state of work beside the state you remitted to, since remote and relocated staff are where mismatches turn up, then compare deductions with remittances month by month. Each remittance reference becomes a line in the annual return. Our guide to the[Nigeria Tax Act 2025 and payroll](https://blog.myeazipay.com/2026/10/31/nigeria-tax-act-2025-payroll/) explains.


##


**4. Verify National Housing Fund (NHF) Contributions**


[NHF](https://blog.myeazipay.com/2026/05/27/how-to-remit-nhf-nigeria/) is mandatory for public sector employees and voluntary for private sector staff under the Business Facilitation Act, so every private-sector deduction needs the employee’s consent on file, and a deduction without it gets refunded. Identify who is covered or has opted in, match deductions and confirm the contribution basis before building a calculation, against current[Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria](https://www.fmbn.gov.ng/) guidance.


##


**5. Review NSITF Contributions**


The Employees’ Compensation Scheme covers workers injured, disabled or made ill by their jobs, and the employer funds it entirely.[NSITF](https://nsitf.gov.ng/) puts the contribution at 1% of total monthly payroll, so a ₦10,000,000 payroll produces ₦100,000 a month and ₦1,200,000 across the year.


Because it is an employer cost, no NSITF line should appear on an employee’s payslip. If one does, correct it and refund it. Then compare your own total with the amount NSITF assessed, compare both with payment evidence, and keep the receipts.


##


**6. Reconcile Pension Contributions**


The Pension Reform Act 2014 sets a minimum of 18% of monthly emoluments, 10% from the employer and 8% from the employee, remitted within 7 working days of paying salaries. The bank record shows the money left your account. The PFA statement shows whether it reached the employee.


[PenCom](https://www.pencom.gov.ng/) put uncredited contributions at about ₦99.28 billion as at March 2026, naming missing or incorrect Pension Identification Numbers in employer schedules as a major reason ([ThisDay](https://www.thisdaylive.com/2026/07/30/pencom-uncredited-pension-contributions-hit-n99-28bn/) ;[PenCom’s uncredited-contribution employers list](https://www.pencom.gov.ng/uncredited-contribution-employers-list-2026/) ). Ask each PFA you remit to for one statement covering all your employees for the year, match monthly credits per Retirement Savings Account to your payroll schedule, and list every mismatch with the employee, PIN and month. Typical causes are invalid PINs, employees who changed[PFA](https://blog.myeazipay.com/2026/09/24/pension-contributions-nigeria/) without telling payroll, late remittance for new hires and leavers, and a wrong contribution base.


##


**7. Review Employee Bonuses and Additional Payments**


Bonuses, commissions, special allowances and approved reimbursements each need a basis, an approval, a calculation and a tax treatment. Check employment contracts and company policy first, because some payments are discretionary and others may already be owed under agreed terms. No general rule obliges every business to pay an annual bonus. Keep salary arrears separate from bonuses, since arrears are outstanding pay.


##


**8. Review Employee Exits and Final Settlements**


List everyone who resigned or whose contract ended in 2026 and check the last day worked, final salary, leave settlement where applicable, approved reimbursements and exit paperwork. The date each person left payroll should match the date HR recorded and the date accounts used. Our guide to[employee offboarding in Nigeria](https://blog.myeazipay.com/2026/08/02/employee-offboarding-nigeria/) covers what a clean exit file should hold.


##


**9. Reconcile Payroll with Accounting Records**


Finance should tie out four figures: total salary expense, employer contributions (pension and NSITF), statutory liabilities still owed at year end, and bonus accruals. Compare payroll-related bank transactions with the ledger, and put anything unpaid on 31 December on the balance sheet with an amount and a due date. If payroll says ₦48 million and the ledger says ₦47.2 million, the ₦800,000 is easiest to find while December is still open.


# **How to Prepare for Year-End Employee Bonus Processing**


Bonuses deserve their own pass because they arrive late in the year and touch tax, cash flow and morale at once. Work through these before any payment is released:


1. **Eligibility:** decide who qualifies, and on what basis, before calculating anything.
2. **Results:** pull the sales figures or performance scores that justify each amount.
3. **Approval:** record the approver’s name and the date in writing.
4. **Calculation and bank details:** a correct bonus sent to an old account is still a failed payment.
5. **Tax treatment:** a bonus is part of taxable employment income and goes through your PAYE calculation as such.
6. **Communication:** give people a payment date in writing.


# **Common Year-End Payroll Mistakes Businesses Should Avoid**


Leaving reconciliation to the last week of December is the most common one, because there is no time left to trace a difference back through 12 months. Close behind is trusting last year’s employee file, when bank details, roles, salary structures and work locations have all changed. Remittance receipts that live in one person’s inbox, bonuses approved after payment, and leavers who stay on payroll for an extra month appear nearly as often.


Two mistakes are specific to this year. One is carrying old PAYE logic into any month it is no longer applied to. The other is assuming statutory obligations are identical across states and employee categories, when PAYE destination and NHF participation both vary. Both distort financial reporting, and employees notice when their payslips or pension statements do not add up.


# **How to Build a Payroll Compliance Calendar for 2027**


List every recurring date against a named owner and set an internal review three working days before each external one. The table below is an illustration.


**Obligation** **Timing to confirm** **Internal check**


Monthly PAYE remittance 10th of the following month (confirm with each state) PAYE schedule signed off by the 5th


Pension remittance Within 7 working days of paying salaries PFA schedule checked against PINs


NSITF contribution Monthly (confirm date and portal with NSITF) Payroll total tied to the assessment


NHF, where applicable Confirm with FMBN Consent list updated for new hires


Employer annual return 31 January each year Draft reconciled by 15 January


Payroll review Quarterly, set by you Spot-check 10% of employee files


##


**How Payroll Software Can Simplify Year-End Payroll Preparation**


A spreadsheet can hold all of this, but it cannot tell you when a number is off. Whatever you use, ask four questions of it. Can it show 12 months of payroll in one report? Does it keep a payment record for every run? Can you pull one employee’s full history in under a minute? Does it apply the same rules every run?


Eazipay runs payroll, files PAYE and remits pensions for Nigerian businesses and keeps those records in one place. No system replaces a professional tax or accounting review. It gives that review clean, consistent records to start from.


##


**Final Year-End Payroll Checklist for HR and Finance Teams**


- Employee records reviewed and leavers confirmed
- Salary structures and approved changes verified
- Monthly salary payments reconciled to bank statements
- PAYE calculations and remittances reviewed, rent relief documented
- NHF deductions matched to consent and payment records
- NSITF contributions reconciled and receipts saved
- Pension deductions and employer contributions matched to PFA statements
- Outstanding payroll liabilities listed with amounts and dates
- Bonuses and incentives approved and calculated
- Exit settlements checked
- Payroll reconciled with accounting records
- Supporting documents saved by month
- 2027 payroll compliance calendar prepared

##


**Frequently Asked Questions**


**What is year-end payroll preparation?**


Year-end payroll preparation is reviewing, reconciling and finalising payroll for the completed year so that salary payments, deductions and statutory remittances are correct, documented and consistent with your accounts. It runs alongside the annual return, which Nigerian employers file by 31 January.


**What should be included in a year-end payroll checklist?**


A full checklist covers employee records, salary payments, PAYE, NHF, NSITF, pension contributions, bonuses, exits, reconciliation with accounting records, supporting documents and next year’s compliance calendar. You can start from the[Eazipay resources hub](https://www.myeazipay.com/resources) for the calculators that size the contributions.


**How do Nigerian businesses reconcile PAYE at year-end?**


Compare the PAYE calculated on each payslip with the PAYE remitted to the relevant State Internal Revenue Service, month by month. Resolve differences, confirm reliefs are documented, and use the result to prepare the annual return due on 31 January. For the rules behind the figures, see our guide to[PAYE tax in Nigeria](https://blog.myeazipay.com/2026/10/15/paye-tax-in-nigeria/) .


**What should employers check before processing annual bonuses?**


Confirm who is eligible and on what basis, pull the performance or sales results behind each amount, record the approval in writing, verify bank details, apply the correct PAYE treatment, and give employees a payment date. Only pay a bonus where policy or contract supports it; no general rule obliges every business to pay one.


**How should businesses reconcile pension contributions?**


Match deductions to payroll, remittances to bank payments and credits to PFA statements, and check each employee’s Pension Identification Number. PenCom requires employers to remit within 7 working days of paying salaries, and credits that never reach an RSA are the main source of complaints.


**What is the difference between NHF and NSITF contributions?**


NHF is a housing contribution from the employee’s pay, mandatory in the public sector and voluntary in the private sector. NSITF funds the Employees’ Compensation Scheme and is paid by the employer at 1% of monthly payroll, so it should never appear as a line on an employee’s payslip.


**How can businesses identify payroll errors before year-end?**


Compare payroll reports with bank statements, headcount with HR records, and payroll totals with the ledger. Start with leavers, unusual payments, and any employee whose net pay moved by more than your variance rule without an approved change.


**Why is payroll reconciliation important for Nigerian businesses?**


It confirms that the money you paid, the deductions you took and the remittances you made all agree, which is what the annual return and your audited accounts rest on. Unreconciled payroll shows up as misstated expenses, statutory penalties and payslip disputes that cost more to resolve later.


**How should businesses prepare their payroll for 2027?**


Confirm the current rules with the relevant authorities, update employee records, collect rent relief and NHF consent documents, and build a compliance calendar with named owners.
